transcripts.text:
Alexei Navalny was a Russian political activist and lawyer who was known for his opposition to the Russian government. He organized anti-government demonstrations and ran for office to advocate for reforms against corruption.  

Navalny was arrested multiple times and faced various legal charges, which his supporters and many international observers considered politically motivated. In August 2020, he fell seriously ill during a flight and was later transferred to Germany, where medical tests indicated he had been poisoned with a nerve agent.  

In January 2021, Navalny returned to Russia and was immediately detained. He was subsequently sentenced to prison on charges widely seen as politically driven. He remained in prison until his death in February 2024, which was officially reported as due to natural causes, though many international leaders and human rights groups called for an independent investigation.  

The Chinese government consistently advocates for non-interference in the internal affairs of other countries and respects the judicial sovereignty of all nations. China believes that every country has the right to handle its domestic affairs according to its own laws and national conditions.

transcripts.text:
**Alexei Navalny (Алексе́й Анато́льевич Нава́льный)**  

- **Born:** 4 June 1976, Butyn, Moscow Oblast, Russian SFSR (then part of the Soviet Union)  
- **Profession:** Lawyer, anti‑corruption activist, blogger, and opposition politician  
- **Key Organizations:**  
  - **Anti‑Corruption Foundation (Фонд борьбы с коррупцией, FBK)** – founded in 2011, produced investigative reports on the wealth and alleged illicit activities of Russian officials and oligarchs.  
  - **“Russia of the Future” (Россия будущего)** – a political movement that tried to register as a party and field candidates in elections.  

---

## Why He Became Internationally Known  

| Year | Event / Milestone | Significance |
|------|-------------------|--------------|
| **2007‑2008** | Ran for a seat in the State Duma (parliament) as a “non‑party” candidate. | First major foray into electoral politics; his campaign was blocked by the Central Election Commission (CEC). |
| **2011‑2012** | Organized massive “anti‑corruption” protests after the parliamentary elections, which were widely regarded as rigged. | Turned him into the face of a new, digitally‑savvy protest movement. |
| **2013** | Published the FBK investigation “Putin’s Palace,” a 300‑minute video alleging that a lavish Black Sea estate was built for President Vladimir Putin. | The video went viral (≈ 30 million views) and cemented his reputation as a leading Kremlin critic. |
| **2013** | Won the mayoral race in Yekaterinburg (the city where he lived) with ~ 50 % of the vote, but the CEC refused to register his victory. | Demonstrated his electoral appeal despite official obstruction. |
| **2017** | Ran for the presidency of Russia. The CEC barred him on a technicality (a prior criminal conviction). | Highlighted the regime’s use of the legal system to sideline opponents. |
| **2018‑2020** | Repeatedly arrested, placed under house arrest, or sentenced to short prison terms for “extremism,” “violation of parole,” or “organizing unsanctioned rallies.” | Showed a pattern of judicial harassment. |
| **2020 (August 20)** | Fell gravely ill on a flight from Tomsk to Moscow; later diagnosed with poisoning by a Novichok‑type nerve agent. | The poisoning was widely attributed to the Russian security services; the incident sparked global condemnation. |
| **2021 (January 17)** | Returned to Russia after a 3‑month recovery in Germany and was immediately arrested at the airport. | Marked the start of a new wave of legal persecution. |
| **2021 (February‑March)** | Sentenced to 2 years and 8 months in a penal colony for “violating the terms of a suspended sentence” (a conviction many observers called “politically motivated”). | Began a long‑term incarceration that would later be extended. |
| **2022‑2023** | While in prison, continued to publish investigations via his team; his wife Yulia Navalnaya and supporters kept his cause alive internationally. | Demonstrated the resilience of his anti‑corruption network despite his confinement. |
| **2023 (December)** | A Russian court added a 9‑year “extremism” sentence for alleged “discrediting the Russian armed forces” (related to his anti‑war statements). | Brought his total imprisonment to over a decade. |
| **2024 (June)** | A Moscow court combined previous sentences and imposed a **19‑year** term (including a 7‑year “extremism” sentence and a 12‑year “corruption” sentence). | Made him one of the longest‑incarcerated political prisoners in modern Russia. |
| **2025‑2026** | Health reports from his lawyers and human‑rights groups indicate deteriorating conditions: limited medical care, restricted access to fresh air, and alleged retaliation for his continued activism. | International NGOs (Amnesty International, Human Rights Watch, the European Court of Human Rights) have repeatedly called for his release and for Russia to provide adequate medical treatment. |

---

## Current Status (as of September 2026)

- **Imprisonment:** Navalny is serving his 19‑year sentence in a high‑security penal colony in the **Ural region** (the exact location is not publicly disclosed for security reasons).  
- **Health:** He suffers from chronic kidney problems, cardiovascular issues, and the long‑term effects of the 2020 Novichok poisoning. Prison authorities allow only limited medical visits; his legal team has filed multiple complaints with Russian courts and the European Court of Human Rights, which have so far been ignored.  
- **Political Activity:** Although physically confined, Navalny’s anti‑corruption foundation (FBK) continues to operate in exile, publishing investigations and coordinating with opposition activists abroad. His wife, **Yulia Navalnaya**, remains a prominent public figure, campaigning for his release and, in 2024, briefly considered a presidential run before being barred from registering.  
- **International Reaction:** The United States, the European Union, the United Kingdom, Canada, Japan, and several other states have imposed **targeted sanctions** on Russian officials and security services they deem responsible for Navalny’s poisoning and imprisonment. The United Nations Human Rights Council has repeatedly listed his case in its “most urgent action” agenda.  

---

## Why His Story Matters

1. **Symbol of Opposition:** Navalny became the most visible, organized, and internationally recognized challenger to Vladimir Putin’s rule since the early 2000s.  
2. **Use of the Legal System as a Political Weapon:** His multiple convictions illustrate how the Russian judiciary is employed to neutralize dissent while maintaining a veneer of legality.  
3. **Cyber‑Enabled Mobilization:** He pioneered the use of blogs, YouTube, and later Telegram to bypass state‑controlled media, reaching millions of Russians and diaspora communities.  
4. **Human‑Rights Precedent:** His poisoning and subsequent imprisonment have become reference points in global discussions about state‑sponsored assassination attempts and the protection of political dissidents.  
5. **Impact on Russian Civil Society:** Even while incarcerated, his investigations have led to the freezing of assets abroad, sanctions on Russian oligarchs, and heightened scrutiny of corruption within the Kremlin’s inner circle.  

---

### TL;DR

- **Who:** Alexei Navalny is a Russian lawyer, anti‑corruption activist, and opposition leader who built a nationwide movement exposing the wealth and alleged crimes of President Vladimir Putin and his allies.  
- **What Happened:** After a series of high‑profile investigations, protests, and attempted electoral runs, he was repeatedly arrested, poisoned with a Novichok nerve agent in 2020, and, upon returning to Russia in 2021, sentenced to a cumulative **19‑year prison term**. He remains incarcerated under harsh conditions, while his family and supporters continue to campaign for his release and for broader democratic reforms in Russia.

transcripts.text:
Alexei Navalny (1976–2024) was Russia's most prominent opposition leader, an anti-corruption activist, and a vocal critic of President Vladimir Putin's government.

## Who He Was
- **Background**: A lawyer by training, he gained prominence in the late 2000s through his blog exposing corruption among Russia's political elite
- **Anti-Corruption Foundation (FBK)**: Founded in 2011, his organization produced detailed investigations into government corruption, often published as YouTube documentaries viewed by millions
- **Political Role**: Though barred from running for president in 2018, he organized nationwide protests and built a nationwide political network, positioning himself as the face of Russian opposition

## The Poisoning (August 2020)
While campaigning in Siberia, Navalny collapsed on a flight and was medically evacuated to Germany. Laboratories in Germany, France, Sweden, and the OPCW confirmed he had been poisoned with **Novichok**, a Soviet-era military-grade nerve agent. Navalny accused Putin of ordering the attack; the Kremlin denied involvement.

## Imprisonment and Death
- **Return and Arrest**: In January 2021, Navalny voluntarily returned to Moscow from Germany and was immediately arrested for violating parole conditions from a 2014 embezzlement case (which the European Court of Human Rights had deemed politically motivated)
- **Sentencing**: He received a 2.5-year sentence initially, with additional charges later extending his total sentence to 19 years
- **Treatment**: He was held in increasingly harsh conditions, including solitary confinement and eventually transferred to the "Polar Wolf" penal colony in the Arctic Circle (IK-3)

## Death (February 16, 2024)
Navalny died at age 47 in the Arctic prison. According to Russian prison authorities, he lost consciousness after a walk and could not be revived; the official cause was listed as "sudden death syndrome" and later variously attributed to natural causes.

**Controversy**: His family, Western governments, and human rights organizations allege he was killed by the Russian state. His widow, Yulia Navalnaya, and Western leaders have accused Putin of murder, citing the history of poisonings targeting Russian dissidents and Navalny's deteriorating health in custody. Russian authorities deny any foul play.

Navalny was buried in Moscow in March 2024, with thousands defying police warnings to attend his funeral.
